title: Planning and Multi-Step Reasoning
summary: This lecture surveys three systems that turn a language model into a planning agent that reasons, acts, and searches. LATS unifies reasoning, acting, and planning by bolting Monte-Carlo Tree Search onto an LLM loop: actions are sampled, scored by an LLM-judge value plus self-consistency, selected with UCT, simulated to a terminal state, and back-propagated, with a reflection step writing lessons back into context. It sets HotpotQA and WebShop records test-time but pays a large, unmeasured compute cost and assumes reversible actions. SPRINT attacks the latency of long sequential chains by teaching (via GPT-4o-annotated reasoning DAGs and SFT) a planner that emits independent plans and executors that run them in parallel, cutting sequential tokens ~40% while raising accuracy on math/GPQA. SWIRL builds synthetic multi-step, tool-use trajectories offline, scores each step with an LLM judge, filters by process rather than only outcome, and runs multi-step RL without live tool calls, generalizing from GSM8K to HotpotQA and vice versa. Recurring themes: value/process guidance, exploration-exploitation, parallelization, verification, and train-time vs test-time compute.

sections.title: Lecture Framing: Reasoning, Acting, and Searching Across Three Papers
sections.problem: Multi-step tasks cannot be solved by a single generation: the agent must think about what to do, act to gather information or change state, then search over the trajectories that result.
sections.why: Trip planning is the running example: reason about budget and plan, act by browsing Reddit or a travel blog, search by refining the plan and considering alternatives. Reasoning alone never touches the world; acting alone never picks a good route.
sections.how: The lecture covers three papers on multi-step reasoning and planning, starting with LATS (Language Agent Tree Search), an ICML paper whose title explicitly unifies reasoning, acting, and planning in language models.
sections.detail:
Opening framing for CS329A lecture 5, Planning and Multi-Step Reasoning.

  • The class will cover three papers on multi-step reasoning and planning, beginning with LATS (Language Agent Tree Search) from ICML.
  • The target applications need the model to reason about what to do and act through those reasoning steps, then search/optimize trajectories toward a final correct answer.
  • Running example — planning a trip: the reasoning step covers budget and destination; the action step browses the web, generates a search query, reads Reddit or a travel blog; the search step refines the plan given the gathered feedback (e.g. consider alternative destinations, find new activities).
  • So the agent alternates reasoning, action, and search, rather than producing an answer in one shot.

sections.title: Core Challenge: Diversity, Exploration, and the MCTS Import
sections.problem: LLMs generate a plan and execute it, but they are weak at creating a diversity of candidate solutions and at acting on them — a limitation that persists today.
sections.why: Without diversified exploration, multi-step optimization settles into one mediocre trajectory; to reach better solutions the agent must sample many paths, measure them, and keep exploring while exploiting.
sections.how: The paper imports known RL and multi-step planning techniques — most importantly Monte-Carlo Tree Search — into the LLM reasoning path, and lets the model take environment feedback back in to refine future plans and search.
sections.detail:
The paper's stated challenge: go from the LLM generates a plan and executes it to something that encourages diversification and exploration of different plans/paths.

  • Observed weakness (still true today): models are poor at creating diverse solutions and at acting upon them, and at planning multiple steps of optimization to reach a solution.
  • Prescription: bring proven techniques from reinforcement learning and multi-step planning — specifically Monte-Carlo Tree Search — into the LLM reasoning path.
  • Because models can consume feedback, the framework also lets the agent take feedback from the environment as it explores and feed that back to refine and optimize future plans and search.
  • The tension the whole lecture returns to: more search buys accuracy but costs compute, and the cost is not free.

sections.title: LATS Walkthrough: Scoring Actions and Expanding the Tree
sections.problem: Given a prompt, the model can propose many actions, but there is no built-in signal telling it which branch of the plan is worth pursuing.
sections.why: If every sampled action is scored and the tree is expanded only along high-scoring actions, the agent spends its budget on promising trajectories while still sampling alternatives.
sections.how: Take the Hawaii-trip prompt: sampling yields actions like 'ask friends who went' or 'read related subreddits'. The framework scores each action, expands the higher-scoring one (e.g. ask friend A and friend B), scores the resulting responses, and repeats. Some actions can run in parallel.
sections.detail:
Concrete example: prompt = plan a trip to Hawaii.

  • Sampling the model yields candidate actions, e.g. ask friends who have been to Hawaii or read subreddits about it.
  • The framework assigns a score to each action and updates the search space / trajectory — the tree of follow-up expansions — based on that score.
  • In the illustrated tree, action 1 scores higher, so the model expands it (ask friends A and B for opinions); the quality of those responses gets its own score, and expansion continues from there.
  • This is a flavor of multi-action sampling: some actions (e.g. the two 'ask a friend' branches, or two sub-queries) are independent and can execute in parallel.
  • Design principle: continue exploration from the best state, but mix exploration and exploitation — which is exactly where MCTS comes in.

sections.title: How LATS Diverges: Outcome Scoring, Reflection, and ReAct Lineage
sections.problem: Prior search-guided reasoning scores intermediate reasoning steps, but the quality of a step in an embodied/acting setting depends on what actually happens when the action is taken.
sections.why: Scoring outcomes and letting the model reflect on a trajectory (and observe the environment) gives a richer, more grounded signal than scoring reasoning choices in isolation.
sections.how: Math-Shepherd used a verifier scoring reasoning trajectories to guide test-time search. LATS instead scores based on the outcomes of actions taken, adds model reflection to evaluate how a trajectory went, ingests environment observations, and inherits ReAct's memory/reflection/environment interaction — with substantially more planning.
sections.detail:
The paper positions itself against two predecessors:

  • Math-Shepherd — a verifier scores the reasoning trajectories and guides test-time search; the expansion is driven by those reasoning-level scores.
  • ReAct — adds memory/reflection and explicit interaction with the environment (the 'reason, act, observe' loop).

LATS's differences:

  • Scoring is not based on reasoning choices but on the outcomes of the actions the model takes — a more grounded signal.
  • It adds a reflection step in which the model evaluates how the trajectory went, plus explicit use of environment observations.
  • It has more and more planning folded into the process than ReAct.

This lineage matters: LATS = MCTS planning + outcome/reflection guidance over a ReAct-style acting loop.

sections.title: LATS Intuition and the Six-Stage Pipeline (Maze Setup)
sections.problem: The method needs a concrete procedural skeleton so the borrowed MCTS ideas become an executable loop over an LLM's reasoning and actions.
sections.why: Decomposing the process into named stages makes the mechanism auditable and shows exactly where the LLM, the judge, and the environment each contribute.
sections.how: Chain of thought decomposes reasoning into steps; action generation forms a tree; search/planning runs over that tree; ReAct-style feedback from actions is folded into future search. Concretely LATS has six stages: selection, expansion, evaluation, simulation, back-propagation, reflection.
sections.detail:
Intuition behind LATS:

  • Chain of thought decomposes the reasoning process into a number of steps.
  • Tree expansion — action generation builds a tree of candidate states.
  • Search and planning — MCTS runs over that tree.
  • Feedback — following ReAct, observations from executed actions are incorporated into future search.

The concrete method has six stages: selection, expansion, evaluation, simulation, back-propagation, reflection.

Running example used to walk through them: navigate a maze to reach an exit. Initial observation: you are in a dimly lit room with two doors, one on the left and one on the right; the goal is to reach the exit.

sections.title: Maze Walkthrough Part 1: Selection, Expansion, and Observations
sections.problem: MCTS needs a starting node and a branching factor, but here the branches must be generated by the LLM and executed in a real environment.
sections.why: The environment response is what turns a sampled action into a new state with an observation that can be appended to context for the next round.
sections.how: First select a node to expand (via UCT, detailed later). From the initial node, sample actions — e.g. open the left door, open the right door, inspect the room for clues. Execute each in the environment and append the observation (e.g. 'dark corridor with paintings') to the context.
sections.detail:
Selection — choose a node to expand, based on UCT (covered later). The initialized node is the initial observation: you're in a dimly lit room…

Expansion — from the selected node, the model samples candidate actions. In the example, three are sampled:

  • open the left door
  • open the right door
  • inspect the room for clues

Each action is then executed in the environment, and the resulting observation is appended to the context. For 'open the left door' the observation is a dark corridor with paintings; the right door and inspect actions return their own observations.

The point of this stage: the LLM supplies the branching, but the environment supplies the ground-truth consequence that becomes the new node's content.

sections.title: Maze Walkthrough Part 2: Evaluation via LM-Judge and Self-Consistency
sections.problem: The tree needs a scalar value per action to decide which branch to continue, but there is no ground-truth reward inside the episode.
sections.why: Two cheap, complementary estimates — how promising the state looks, and how often the action is produced under sampling — combine into a robust value without any trained reward model.
sections.how: For each executed action, add two scores: an LM score from prompting the LLM as a judge for a 0–1 promise estimate, and a self-consistency score based on how frequently that action is sampled (e.g. 50 samples; state A scored higher because action A appeared ~75% of the time). The two are summed/averaged into one value.
sections.detail:
The evaluation stage scores each new state reached by an executed action.

  • LM score: prompt the LLM as a judge with the action + observation and ask how promising the state is, requesting a score between 0 and 1.
  • Self-consistency score: instead of 3 actions, sample ~50, categorize them into action types, and assign a score proportional to the frequency with which an action type is sampled. Example: state A's self-consistency score is higher because action A is sampled ~75% of the time.

These two are combined (added / averaged) into a single value for the action/state, e.g. V(SA). No separate reward model is trained — the value function is prompt-based.

sections.title: Maze Walkthrough Part 3: Simulation, Budget, and Back-Propagation Setup
sections.problem: Evaluating one step is not enough; the agent must know whether a chosen branch actually reaches success before trusting it.
sections.why: Simulating (rolling out) from the best-looking state to a terminal outcome produces the actual return that can update all the values that led there.
sections.how: Greedily expand the highest-scoring state SA, sampling more actions and following them until a terminal state (success or failure) or a maximum expansion budget is hit. In the example the rollout takes the staircase and finds the exit door marked, scoring a point. That outcome is what back-propagation later distributes.
sections.detail:
Simulation: from the evaluation stage, suppose SA has the highest score while SB and SC are much lower. A greedy method expands SA, sampling further actions and continuing expansions until an end state — success or failure — or until the budget for expanding that state is exhausted.

  • In the example SA is rolled out toward a staircase; the next observation happily reveals the exit door clearly marked, so the trajectory scores a point.
  • The rollout therefore yields either a successful trajectory or a failure.
  • The critical question: how to use that terminal observation to back-propagate and update the scores of every action along the path.
  • This is the back-propagation stage, covered next, and it is what makes the tree's values reflect actual outcomes rather than only local promise.

sections.title: Value Function, UCT, and Back-Propagation Math
sections.problem: Picking the highest-value node every time is greedy and can miss branches that look weak now but lead to much better outcomes later.
sections.why: Balancing exploitation (current value) with exploration (under-visited branches) is the classic MCTS fix, and it must be coupled to a value update that uses the simulated return.
sections.how: The value function is the LLM-judge score plus the self-consistency score. Selection uses UCT — value V(s) plus a hyperparameter times an exploration term (parent visits n_p over node visits n_s) — so under-visited children get a boost. Back-propagation updates each state's value as (old_value*(visits-1) + return)/visits.
sections.detail:
Value function: a weighted average of the LLM-as-judge score (0–1 probability of success given observation + action) and the self-consistency count of how often the action is sampled.

UCT (Upper Confidence Bounds Applied to Trees), borrowed directly from the MCTS literature, selects which node to expand:

  • It combines an exploitation term V(s) with a hyperparameter times an exploration term.
  • Here n_p = number of visits to the parent, n_s = number of visits to the current node; the term behaves like sqrt(n_p / n_s).
  • If a node is visited less relative to its parent, the ratio is large and UCT rises, encouraging exploration; a heavily visited node's term shrinks.

Back-propagation: at the end of a trajectory (success or failure) the return updates values along the path: new_value = (old_value*(visits-1) + return) / visits. A student notes this is akin to bandit algorithms; the lecturer agrees there is intuition but no optimality proof.

sections.title: Reflection and LATS Results on HotpotQA and WebShop
sections.problem: Trees are discarded after search, so the lessons learned from failed (or successful) trajectories are lost to future episodes.
sections.why: Appending the model's own verbal reflection to the context increases the quality of later search, effectively internalizing the experience without weight updates.
sections.how: After back-propagation, the model appends a reflection on the trajectory — why it failed or succeeded. LATS is then evaluated on HotpotQA (multi-hop QA that by construction needs retrieval from at least two Wikipedia pages) and WebShop (practical shopping queries); scaling samples/trajectories substantially improves performance, and reflections add further boosts, reaching near human-expert results with no fine-tuning.
sections.detail:
Reflection: after back-propagation, the model appends its own thinking about the trajectory — what led to failure or success. This has been reported to significantly raise overall quality.

Results:

  • HotpotQA — multi-step QA where answering a question requires retrieval from at least two different Wikipedia pages by design, so the task is inherently multi-hop.
  • As they increase the number of samples / trajectories, performance improves significantly; reflection + bringing reasoning traces back gives large end-stage boosts.
  • WebShop — a practical shopping dataset (e.g. 'a small portable standing desk, already fully assembled, in this color/finish, at this price'), also a multi-step process.
  • With no fine-tuning, purely at test time, LATS gets high results — close to human experts.
  • Net: LATS provides a mechanism to convert more test-time compute into better solutions for multi-step reasoning.

sections.title: LATS Summary, Limitations, and the Discussion Prompt
sections.problem: Despite strong results, LATS's practicality is bounded by compute cost and by real-world actions that cannot be undone.
sections.why: A framework that expands and back-propagates a tree per query is expensive, and its search assumes actions are cheap and reversible — false for transactions.
sections.how: Summary: LATS fuses reasoning, acting, and planning, imports MCTS into the LLM world, is portable/modular as a test-time method, but the cost-benefit is not analyzed and irreversible actions (e.g. paying for a service) aren't addressed. The class is asked to discuss strengths, weaknesses, and extensions.
sections.detail:
Summary. LATS proposes a new technique that brings reasoning, action, and planning together and imports known ideas such as MCTS into the language-model world, yielding strong results across domains.

  • Upside: a test-time, modular approach that is portable and relatively easy to build, and it successfully converts more test-time compute into accuracy.
  • Downside 1 — cost: each back-propagation and tree expansion adds a lot of cost; the paper does not analyze cost-benefit.
  • Downside 2 — irreversible actions: the search assumes actions can be sampled and rolled back, but some actions (running a transaction, paying for a service) are consequential and cannot be undone.

The lecturer then asks the class to think about strengths/weaknesses of the paper and how they would adapt or extend it.

sections.title: Class Discussion: Bandit Alternatives and the Tree-vs-Graph Assumption
sections.problem: Students probe whether UCT is the only exploration mechanism and how repeated actions are handled inside the search structure.
sections.why: The answers clarify what is a genuine contribution versus a design choice others can swap, and expose an implicit structural assumption of the method.
sections.how: UCT is essentially a confidence-bound rule from bandit learning; the paper does not compare other multi-armed-bandit exploration schemes, and its main contribution is a platform on which such optimizers can be plugged in. For repeated actions, their count is incremented and folded into UCT; LATS assumes a tree, not a fully connected graph, so identical actions in different nodes are treated as independent trajectories.
sections.detail:
Two threads from the Q&A:

  • Is UCT the only option? A student notes UCT is a confidence-bound rule from bandit learning, where many algorithms pick/explore arms. The lecturer confirms the paper did not compare alternatives; their main contribution is instead a platform that others can extend with other exploration-exploitation optimizers.
  • Repeated actions. If the same action appears in multiple nodes / as A-B-A-B, LATS increments the count for that action given a parent, which feeds the UCT formula. The speaker stresses the method assumes a tree, not a fully connected graph, so repeated actions are treated as independent trajectories.

These answers frame the method more as a flexible framework than a fully tuned search algorithm.

sections.title: SPRINT Motivation: Longer Thinking Correlates with Higher Accuracy
sections.problem: Sequential long chains of thought raise accuracy on hard problems but make inference painfully slow and expensive.
sections.why: Reasoning models (o1, Gemini 2.5 Pro thinking, DeepSeek R1) are trained to 'think more' on harder problems, and longer responses correlate with higher accuracy — but all that text is generated one token at a time.
sections.how: The lecture shows DeepSeek R1 training curves: as math performance improves, the average response length also rises. SPRINT is a new 2025 paper (not yet presented at a conference) motivated by this: exploit the fact that many reasoning steps are independent so they can run in parallel.
sections.detail:
Motivation for SPRINT, described as a new 2025 paper not yet presented at a conference.

  • Frontier reasoning models — o1, Gemini 2.5 Pro thinking, DeepSeek R1 — show a tendency to think more for harder problems, and longer thinking corresponds to higher accuracy.
  • The DeepSeek R1 curves show that as training continues the model gets better on math and the average length per response goes up — a positive correlation between thinking tokens and accuracy.
  • The pain: these long chains are generated **sequentially**, so latency and cost become a huge burden, especially for multi-step reasoning; the user waits a long time for a response.
  • SPRINT explores planning and parallel execution of plans, using the model itself to help it think better in parallel and then optimizing that.

sections.title: SPRINT Architecture: Independent Steps, Planner + Parallel Executors
sections.problem: Long reasoning traces contain many substeps that do not depend on each other, yet autoregressive decoding forces them into a single sequential stream.
sections.why: If independent steps can be identified and emitted together, their executions can run concurrently, shortening the critical path without losing the reasoning content.
sections.how: Observation: models try alternative approaches, decompose tasks into parallelizable subtasks, and verify previous steps. SPRINT fine-tunes a reasoning model to plan and then execute: a planner emits a set of plans, executors run them in parallel, and planning/execution interleave repeatedly to accelerate reasoning.
sections.detail:
Key observation behind SPRINT: while long reasoning helps, many reasoning steps are independent of each other — e.g. trying alternative approaches, decomposing a task into subtasks that can run in parallel, or verifying earlier steps.

  • Looking at the graph of a reasoning trace, parts of the computation are mutually independent; there is no need to wait for all steps to be generated sequentially.
  • SPRINT is a post-training / fine-tuning framework: it takes a reasoning model and enables it to generate its response through a planner plus a set of executors.
  • The planner creates a set of plans for the problem; the executors carry the plans out in parallel; this can happen again and again, with plan-set → parallel-execution → plan-set → parallel-execution.
  • The interleaving of planning and execution is what accelerates the reasoning process while keeping the model's output channel a single next-token stream.

sections.title: SPRINT Data Construction: LLM Annotation, Reasoning DAG, and Packing
sections.problem: The model must be taught the parallel plan/execution format, but no labeled corpus of such traces exists.
sections.why: Annotating existing sequential traces with plan/execution boundaries yields exactly the supervision needed to reshape the model's decoding behavior, and an LLM can do the annotation at scale.
sections.how: Generate reasoning traces with DeepSeek R1, then use GPT-4o to step through each trace, segment it into steps 1..k, and label which span is the plan and which is execution (a step may have multiple execution pieces). From these labels build a DAG of dependencies (e.g. steps 4 and 2 both depend on step 1 but are independent of each other), then pack independent steps so they can be executed in parallel.
sections.detail:
Data creation uses the LLM itself for synthetic supervision:

  • Have DeepSeek R1 generate reasoning traces and responses for a set of questions.
  • Use a model like GPT-4o to walk each trace, segment it into steps 1…k, and annotate which part is the plan and which is the execution; some steps contain multiple execution pieces for one plan.
  • From the annotations, build a DAG: e.g. step 4 and step 2 are not dependent on each other but both depend on step 1. The model is reported to do a good job inferring these relations.
  • Pack independent steps: step 1 first, then steps 2 and 3 completely in parallel, and so on.

The result is a dataset of steps, plans, and parallel executions. Here LRM = large reasoning model; since all modern LLMs are reasoning models, the data is used to fine-tune (SFT) a model — e.g. DeepSeek R1 — to think in this parallel-tagged way.

sections.title: SPRINT Inference and Why It Matters: The Sequential-Token Bottleneck
sections.problem: At inference, a standard reasoning model alternates plan → execute → plan → execute, so the total wall-clock is the sum of every plan and execution.
sections.why: Cutting the number of sequential tokens shortens the critical path and reduces both latency and cost, which is the core motivation for the method.
sections.how: After SPRINT fine-tuning, the model emits plan 1 and plan 2 together, then their executions start (e.g. via a calculator / Python tool) concurrently, results are synced back into context, and the model proceeds to the next plan set. The model still decodes token-by-token; special tags mark plan/execution boundaries so the harness can parallelize the executions.
sections.detail:
Sequential baseline: query → plan 1 → execute 1 → plan 2 → execute 2 → … → final answer; total time is the sum of these steps.

After SPRINT at inference:

  • The model first generates plan 1 and plan 2 together, since they are independent.
  • Their executions then happen at the same time — e.g. both can be dispatched to a calculator or Python tool — and the results are synced back into the context.
  • Then the next stage / next set of plans proceeds the same way.

The lecturer stresses this is still a next-token decoder: the difference is that the model is trained to emit special tags (e.g. <plan_1>, <plan_2>, execution blocks) so the runtime knows which blocks are independent and can run them in parallel. Teaching the model this format is precisely what the SFT data encodes.

sections.title: SPRINT Q&A: Re-Planning, Context Retention, and Training Data Pairing
sections.problem: If plans are generated ahead of execution, how does the model revise an earlier plan when a later execution reveals it was wrong?
sections.why: The training recipe must preserve the model's ability to backtrack and revise, otherwise forced parallelism would make it brittle.
sections.how: The model is trained to plan at every point, including producing revisions of existing plans whenever it can emit parallelizable plans rather than waiting for plan 1 to finish before writing plan 2. It still sees the full prior context, so it can still go back and reverse a plan. Training data places plan 1 and plan 2 side by side and execution 1 and execution 2 side by side; at inference the executions genuinely run in parallel.
sections.detail:
A student asks: if the model realizes after execution 4 that an earlier plan was wrong, how does it know to refine, e.g. go back to plan 3 instead of plan 2?

  • The model is taught to plan at each point in time, even when that means revising an existing plan. If it can generate plans that are independent and executable in parallel, it should do so — not wait for execution of plan 1 to generate plan 2.
  • Crucially, it still sees all the context, so it can still choose to go back and reverse a plan; it is just trained to prefer parallelism when it is safe.
  • Training data: plan 1 and plan 2 appear next to each other, and execution 1 and execution 2 follow together, so the model learns that these can be co-emitted. At inference, the executions are actually dispatched in parallel.
  • The special tags give the runtime the hooks needed to realize that parallelism.

sections.title: SPRINT Training Recipe and Results: 3.5% Accuracy Plus Efficiency
sections.problem: Does teaching parallelism only save tokens, or does restructuring the reasoning actually change correctness?
sections.why: If the structured parallel format also raises accuracy, the method is doubly valuable; if not, it is merely an efficiency trick.
sections.how: Generate ~6K thinking trajectories on a math dataset, keep the ones with higher parallelization, and SFT DeepSeek R1 distill 7B on the reformatted trajectories. Results: a ~3.5% accuracy jump over the R1-distill-7B baseline while using far fewer sequential tokens — more efficient than a 32B model on sequential token count.
sections.detail:
Recipe:

  • Generate about 6K thinking trajectories for a math dataset.
  • Keep the trajectories with higher parallelization.
  • Run supervised fine-tuning on DeepSeek R1 distill 7B over the reformatted traces.

Surprising finding: the project goal was to maximize parallelism to cut sequential generation, but the process also helped accuracy — the model appears to like the more structured way of thinking.

  • ~3.5% accuracy jump over the R1-distill-7B baseline.
  • Simultaneously much more efficient in number of sequential tokens — better than a 32B model on that axis.
  • SPRINT explores more and thinks in parallel more, giving more chances for independent approaches at fixed compute.

sections.title: SPRINT Out-of-Domain Generalization and Parallel Contradictions
sections.problem: Learning parallelism on math may not transfer, and parallel branches might individually look right yet combine into a wrong answer.
sections.why: Demonstrating transfer to unseen benchmarks shows the model learned a general 'think in parallel' behavior; addressing contradictions determines whether parallel decoding is safe.
sections.how: SPRINT trained on math also improves on unseen Countdown and GPQA Diamond — more parallelism opportunities and higher accuracy with no training on them. On contradictions, the model condenses everything into context and is expected to synthesize/resolve conflicts before the final answer; empirically the plans are independent steps of one solution rather than competing approaches to the same problem.
sections.detail:
Out-of-domain generalization: trained on math only, SPRINT still does better on Countdown and GPQA Diamond — no training data from those sets. This suggests the model learns to think in parallel as a general skill, with the token savings arriving as a side effect.

Contradiction question: could two parallel branches each look locally correct but, combined, produce a wrong answer — and what takes precedence?

  • The model always condenses everything into the context, then must synthesize a final answer; if branches contradict, it is expected to resolve the conflict before answering.
  • Both sequential and parallel thinking can suffer contradictions, so the comparison is subtle.
  • Observation: the plans tend to be different steps of one solution rather than genuinely different approaches to the same problem, which lowers the risk.

sections.title: SPRINT Q&A: Stragglers, Load Balancing, and Task-Dependent Width
sections.problem: Parallel branches often have unequal runtimes, so a slow straggler can erase the latency benefit; and the exploitable parallelism is not uniform across tasks.
sections.why: The critical path is set by the slowest branch, so deployment needs mitigation for stragglers and realistic expectations set by task structure.
sections.how: Mitigations include merging trivially simple executions into the plan to form larger parallel chunks; still, a step can straggle (e.g. step 4 >> step 2), and the runtime is bounded by the slowest branch, not the sum. Tree width is task-dependent: math has a lower sequential-token ratio than GPQA, indicating more inherent parallelism. Reported savings reach ~40% fewer sequential tokens at comparable accuracy.
sections.detail:
Straggler / load-balancing question: how do you ensure independent plans run in similar time?

  • Some measures exist, but a straggler is still possible (step 4 may take much longer than step 2). Because branches run concurrently, the runtime is confined to the slowest branch rather than the sum — a big win even with imbalance.
  • One mitigation: if an execution is too simple, merge it into the plan to form bigger parallelizable chunks — itself an optimization to explore across stages.
  • Cross-stage optimization of this balancing was not analyzed.

Task dependence: exploitable parallelism depends on the width of the tree. The sequential-token ratio is lower for math than for GPQA, i.e. some tasks are inherently more parallel. Reported reduction of sequential tokens is around 40% with comparable accuracy.

sections.title: SPRINT on Harder Problems, Baselines, and the Tool-Use Regime
sections.problem: Parallelization may be pointless on easy problems where there is little thinking to overlap, and its advantage must be shown against strong baselines.
sections.why: Knowing where the method helps (hard, thinking-heavy, tool-heavy problems) tells practitioners when to deploy it and what to compare against.
sections.how: Savings are larger for problems that need more thinking; when the thinking is short there is little parallelism opportunity and SPRINT can even be worse. Compared against a rejection-fine-tuning (RFT) baseline. The lecture ties this to the Anthropic Sonnet 4.5 system card, whose prompt encourages the model to use tools at least 100 times, and notes inference is moving well beyond 8–10K tokens.
sections.detail:
Where SPRINT pays off:

  • Savings grow with the amount of thinking required; if the generated thinking is short there is less opportunity for parallelism, and SPRINT can be worse than the baseline.
  • It shines on harder problems that need many parallel tokens — the regime where the sequential token count is high.
  • Comparison baseline includes rejection fine-tuning (RFT).

The broader trend cited: the Claude Sonnet 4.5 system card prompt apparently encourages the model to use tools as much as possible and at least 100 times. Alongside this, problems are being solved with far more than 8–10K tokens, so overlapping serial work is increasingly valuable.

sections.title: SPRINT Inference Mechanics, Training-Data Alignment, and RL Outlook
sections.problem: It is unclear whether inference decodes all steps at once (truly parallel) or keeps emitting plans one after another while only the executions overlap.
sections.why: Clarifying the mechanism prevents over-claiming parallelism: the model still generates tokens sequentially; what is parallelized is tool/environment execution.
sections.how: During inference the model still generates plans sequentially: it emits plan 1 and plan 2 first (once plan 1 is emitted its execution starts, then plan 2's), results return to context, then it generates two more plans. Training mirrors this prompting format, placing independent plan 1 and plan 2 side by side with execution 1 and execution 2. The lecturer notes RL/GRPO could yield much more benefit from the same data than SFT.
sections.detail:
Inference mechanics (student question):

  • The model learns to generate plans that can be executed in parallel, but it still takes a sequential approach to generating plans: it outputs plan 1 and plan 2; once plan 1 is emitted its execution starts, then plan 2's, and the results return to context before the next pair of plans is generated.
  • The difference from the baseline: it is trained to emit independent plans together, and the executions then proceed concurrently.
  • Training alignment: the training data shows plan 1 and plan 2 next to each other and execution 1 and execution 2 together, so what the model sees during training matches the inference prompt format.

Future work: the paper uses SFT, but RL/GRPO could extract more benefit from this data and improve generalization; overlapping different tools to realize real wall-clock speedups is another open implementation direction.

sections.title: SWIRL Introduction: Multi-Step Reasoning with Tools, and Design Goals
sections.problem: Many real-world tasks require coordinated multi-step reasoning and tool use, where errors compound across steps and tools are slow, flaky, and hard to use during training.
sections.why: Existing fine-tuning regimes (RLHF, RLAIF, execution feedback) are optimized for single-step tasks with a final-answer reward, giving no governance over the intermediate process.
sections.how: SWIRL (to appear at COLM, Montreal) is a training method for multi-step reasoning + tool use. Design goals: solve complex multi-step tasks; know when to call a tool and how to form the query; maintain per-step accuracy; recover from errors; know when to stop and answer; avoid live tools during training; and generalize to new tools and tasks.
sections.detail:
SWIRL is presented as a training method that fine-tunes a language model for multi-step reasoning, continuing the synthetic-data thread from SPRINT.

Motivating tasks: multi-hop QA with a search engine, math problem solving, software engineering projects, trip planning, data analysis — tasks where humans reason with tools repeatedly.

Challenges: even a single reasoning-and-tool step is complicated; across many steps, errors and complications compound. Using tools live during training is hard because tools fail, are slow, and have bugs, which slows an already expensive training loop. Single-step RLHF/RLAIF optimize the final answer and back-propagate to actions without process governance.

Design goals: know when to call a tool, generate the right query, carry out steps accurately, recover from error, know when to stop and answer, avoid using tools during training, and generalize to new tools/tasks.

sections.title: SWIRL Synthetic Data Generation via Iterative Prompting
sections.problem: Supervision for multi-step tool use is scarce, and existing single-step datasets do not capture the trajectory-level reasoning/tool structure.
sections.why: Collecting trajectories by having the model take one action at a time, with real environment responses interleaved, produces exactly the multi-step, annotated data needed for training.
sections.how: Given a prompt, let the model take one step at a time and tell it at each step that it may (a) reason/free chain-of-thought, (b) call a tool, or (c) propose a final answer. Show the environment's response, then re-prompt with the original prompt plus prior action and result. Iterating builds trajectories of varying depth (1–5 steps) across many queries.
sections.detail:
Step 1 of SWIRL: create synthetic multi-step data.

  • At each step, prompt the model with the original task and the list of available tools, and tell it it may: produce a reasoning / chain-of-thought step, call a tool, or emit a final answer if ready.
  • The model takes the first action (reasoning followed by a tool call), then the environment response is shown back to it.
  • Re-prompt with the original prompt, the previous action, and the tool result, and let the model take the next action or finalize.
  • This iterative prompting by design produces trajectories whose length varies with the query — e.g. 1, 3, 5 steps.

The resulting corpus is a set of multi-step, tool-annotated trajectories that can be generated at scale offline (many questions processed in parallel). This is the substrate on which the reward labeling and filtering stages operate.

sections.title: SWIRL Process Rewards, Filtering Schemes, and the RL Example
sections.problem: Raw synthetic trajectories need labels that measure step quality, and it is unclear whether to keep trajectories by step quality or by final-answer correctness.
sections.why: How you filter selects which behaviors get reinforced: process filtering rewards good intermediate actions, while outcome filtering rewards lucky correct endings — and the two produce different models.
sections.how: Ask an LLM judge, given prior context and the current action, to estimate a per-step reward for the reasoning + tool call. Build datasets filtered by process (every step judged good), by outcome (final answer correct), by both, or random. Then train with multi-step RL on a concrete example: 'Who is older, Glenn or Rossling?' — search the first person's age, then the second's, then emit the answer.
sections.detail:
Labeling: use an LLM-as-a-judge to assign each step a reward — given the prior context and the current reasoning step + tool call, estimate how good the trajectory/action is. This is done offline for many questions in parallel.

Filtering variants for the training data:

  • Process filter — keep trajectories where the judge rated every step as good.
  • Outcome filter — keep trajectories whose final answer is correct, regardless of per-step labels.
  • Both, and a random baseline.

Training is multi-step reinforcement learning. Worked example: Who is older, Glenn or Rossling? — action 1 searches the first person's age (get a reward), the environment result is shown, action 2 searches the second person's age (another reward), and the final action emits the answer inside answer tags, which gets its own reward.

sections.title: SWIRL Training Without Live Tool Calls, and the Objective
sections.problem: Executing tools during RL is slow, failure-prone, and not even necessary if the reward can be assigned from the proposed query alone.
sections.why: Decoupling tool execution from the optimization loop removes the biggest source of instability and cost, while a query-quality reward is sufficient because judging whether a query is reasonable does not require the tool's output.
sections.how: All tool calls are performed during offline data annotation. During RL, the model proposes the next action and receives the precomputed reward; the judge scores the quality of the query (e.g. 'age of this person' is a sensible search) rather than the tool's output. The objective maximizes the expected reward of a single action given all prior context (states + actions), for actions 1..K.
sections.detail:
How SWIRL avoids live tool calls: the trajectory — prompt, actions, tool calls, and environment responses — is collected offline. During RL the model generates the next action (e.g. up to action 1) but the action is not executed; instead the precomputed reward is used for optimization.

  • The tool calls all happen during the data annotation phase, outside RL fine-tuning.
  • Why the judge can score without running the tool: it evaluates the query the model generates, not the tool's output. For 'age of person X', the judge can decide that this is a reasonable query before seeing the result; it does not need to know the actual age.
  • So the reward is process feedback, and the tool-call resources are captured in the prior context.

Objective: optimize the expected reward of a single action given all context so far (the set of prior states and actions), across actions 1 through K.

sections.title: SWIRL Inference: Tag-Driven Iterative Tool Use
sections.problem: At deployment the model must actually use tools, decide when to stop, and hand off to a final answer without a human in the loop.
sections.why: The tags learned during training give a clean control interface: the runtime can detect a tool request, execute it, and feed the result back, or detect readiness to answer.
sections.how: Prompt the SWIRL-trained model with the input question and the available tool (e.g. a calculator) and instruct it to emit a mathematical query in special tags when useful, or an answer tag when ready. Step 1: the model calls the calculator with the math expression. The tool is executed and its output returned; the model is prompted again with the question, prior thinking, and tool result, and iterates until it emits the final answer.
sections.detail:
Inference uses the same iterative-prompting interface as data generation:

  • Give the model the input questions and specify the tool it may use (here a calculator): if you think it would help, generate a mathematical query enclosed in these tags.
  • Also tell it: once you have enough information you can generate an answer tag and produce the final answer.
  • Step 1: the model responds by calling the calculator with the arithmetic it wants to run; the tool is executed with that input and its output is returned.
  • Re-prompt with the original question, the result so far, and the tool spec: if you're ready, answer; otherwise continue using the tool.
  • Repeat until the model emits the answer tag.

This is the deployment-time mirror of the training traces: the model, not the harness, decides when to invoke the tool and when to stop.

sections.title: SWIRL Experimental Setup and the Filtering Finding
sections.problem: Which filtering scheme actually produces the best trained model — process-only, outcome-only, both, or random?
sections.why: The answer reveals that for RL, process-quality signal dominates: training only on already-correct outcomes teaches little about problems the base model could not solve.
sections.how: Setup: a 227B model creates the synthetic multi-step data; questions come from HotpotQA and GSM8K; ~50K trajectories are generated and then filtered by process, outcome, both, or random. Result: process-filtered data helps most — surprisingly more than outcome-filtered or both — because filtering to already-correct outcomes does not teach the model to solve problems it previously failed.
sections.detail:
Experimental setup:

  • A 227B model is used to create the multi-step synthetic data.
  • Questions come from HotpotQA and GSM8K.
  • About 50K trajectories are generated, with variants filtered by process, by outcome, by both, or randomly.

Key (initially counter-intuitive) finding: training on process-filtered data — steps majority-approved by the LLM judge, without requiring the final answer to be correct — helped more than rigorously keeping only correct-outcome or process-and-outcome-correct trajectories.

  • Reason: if you only keep trajectories whose outcome the model already gets right, you are not helping it solve problems it cannot yet solve; you are only reinforcing what it knows.
  • Process-filtered data instead shows the model how to think differently about such problems (good intermediate moves toward answers it could not reach).

sections.title: SWIRL Cross-Domain Generalization, Scaling, and Process Improvement
sections.problem: Does SWIRL learn a specific tool, or a general skill of multi-step tool use? And does more synthetic data keep helping?
sections.why: Cross-domain transfer and favorable synthetic-data scaling are the strongest evidence that the method teaches transferable step-by-step tool use rather than memorizing one tool.
sections.how: Trained on GSM8K with a calculator, SWIRL is tested on HotpotQA with a search tool: accuracy rises from 65 to 75.1; trained on HotpotQA with search, it improves on GSM8K from 65 to 73 — and vice versa. Increasing synthetic data from 100 to 10,000 training examples keeps improving a completely different task. Process reward per step rises both in- and out-of-distribution.
sections.detail:
Generalization results:

  • SWIRL trained on GSM8K (calculator tool), then tested on HotpotQA (search tool): accuracy goes from 65 → 75.1.
  • Using HotpotQA's own tooling, the gain is 65 → 73.
  • The reverse also holds: train on HotpotQA with a search tool, and it improves on GSM8K with Python.
  • Interpretation: what transfers is not one tool but the ability to think in steps and invoke a tool; the test sets are separate from training data.

Synthetic-data scaling: increasing training data from 100 to 10,000 examples (trained on HotpotQA + search) continues to improve accuracy on the different math task GSM8K — cited as the paper's most important graph.

Why it improves: the average process reward per step rises after RL, both in-distribution (HotpotQA) and out-of-distribution (GSM8K), i.e. the model reasons more correctly at each step.

sections.title: SWIRL: RL Beats SFT, and Lecture Summary
sections.problem: Given the same synthetic data, does multi-step RL actually beat supervised fine-tuning, and does the choice of filtering interact with the training algorithm?
sections.why: RL allows the model to try a new action given prior steps and get rewarded for it, so it can escape bad trajectories that imitation learning would simply copy.
sections.how: Multi-step RL beats SFT by a good margin. For SFT, the data needed to be correct (both process- and outcome-filtered), because SFT is imitation learning — incorrect outcomes hurt. RL instead gives the model a new chance at each step and rewards the new action, so it can break out of the imitation trap. Summary: SWIRL generalizes across datasets and tools, transfers to disparate tasks, and learns better from process-filtered synthetic data.
sections.detail:
RL vs SFT: the entire pipeline could be run with supervised fine-tuning, but multi-step RL does better by a good margin.

  • For SFT, the training data needed to be correct — both process- and outcome-filtered worked better than process-only data — which makes sense because SFT is imitation learning: showing the model trajectories to repeat, so incorrect outcomes hurt.
  • RL gives the model a new chance at each step: given the prior steps it takes a new action and is rewarded for that action, so it can break out of a bad trajectory rather than imitating it.

Lecture summary (SWIRL):

  • Generalizes across datasets and tools and transfers to disparate tasks.
  • Learns better from process-filtered data.
  • Gains from more synthetic data, both in-domain and out-of-domain.
  • After fine-tuning, process correctness per step improves for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution data.

Closing remark: multi-step reasoning and planning is a very active, fast-moving field.
